channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - All Critical Infrastructure
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] UK government confirms a cyberattack took a generator offline — and is rewriting the sector’s cyber rules
item.description: Further reporting on 24 August firms up the picture: a small UK generating site was taken offline for four days, in what officials describe as the first successful cyberattack of its kind on British energy infrastructure. The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero confirms a cyberattack impacted a small-scale energy generator, stresses the national grid was never at risk, and — the part defenders should note — says sector cybersecurity regulations are now being updated. The Iran attribution and the four-day duration remain press-sourced; the NCSC has not commented. The affected site sat below the threshold at which generators must report cyber incidents. That exposed population is embedded generation, CHP and district energy, standby and peaking plant, battery storage and small renewables — unmanned assets reached through vendor remote access or a cellular router, sitting under the regulatory floor. Regulators are now moving that floor. - On-record statement from the UK Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, reported via Irish Times, IBTimes UK, CNBC and Security Affairs; duration and attribution from Sunday Telegraph - Telegraph report published 22 Aug 2026; DESNZ statement and CEO briefing 23 Aug 2026; further reporting and international pickup 24 Aug 2026; attack reported as occurring in July 2026, exact date not published

item.title: [Critical] The S7 advisory’s real finding: attackers are running AI-written exploitation scripts dressed up as OT monitoring tools
item.description: Joint advisory AA26-231A, published 19 August by NSA, CISA, the FBI, DOE and EPA, says threat actors are running AI-generated Python scripts — packaged to look like ordinary OT monitoring software — to find and reach Siemens S7 controllers across US critical infrastructure. The tooling is built on the snap7.dll and python-snap7 libraries and speaks S7comm, giving read and write access to PLC memory, configuration data and ladder logic. Targets are located through internet-wide scanning services, then reached through exposed interfaces, outdated firmware or weak authentication. S7-200, S7-300, S7-400, S7-1200 and S7-1500 are all named, across critical manufacturing, energy, water and wastewater, chemical, food and agriculture, and commercial facilities. The agencies assess the activity as persistent reconnaissance and capability development positioning actors for later disruption, say the targeting is broader than Siemens, and state plainly that this is not a theoretical risk. The related campaign against water-sector controllers is where the confirmed damage sits: attackers modified or deleted project-file logic, manipulated HMI and SCADA display data, and disabled shutdown and alarm functions, creating unsafe conditions with no operator notification. - NSA / CISA / FBI / DOE / EPA joint advisory AA26-231A, building on AA26-097A and the FBI water-sector alert — via CISA, BleepingComputer, Help Net Security - AA26-231A published 19 Aug 2026, re-verified 24 Aug 2026 22:00 ET; AA26-097A published 7 Apr 2026, updated 22 Jul 2026; 12-state total through 14 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] CERT Polska: an attacker crossed a shared private cellular network from a wind farm into a heating plant and stopped its turbine
item.description: After an investigation running more than three months, CERT Polska disclosed on 8 August what it assesses to be the first real-world case of an attacker reaching an OT network through a private APN. The intrusion began at a wind farm’s edge, moved onto a cellular router, and crossed a distribution system operator’s private access point name — a dedicated mobile network the DSO had provisioned with a carrier — into a controller at an entirely unrelated combined heat and power plant. The APN was configured to let arbitrary devices on it talk to one another, so what everyone involved treated as a segmentation boundary behaved as a flat shared LAN. At the CHP plant the attacker stopped a steam turbine and the water treatment system that produces process water, interrupting cogeneration at a facility supplying heat to roughly 50,000 residents. The incident itself occurred on 29 December 2025; the disclosure and the technical detail are new this month, and the design pattern it breaks is one agencies have actively recommended. - CERT Polska incident follow-up report — via Help Net Security, BleepingComputer, SecurityWeek, The Hacker News - Incident 29 Dec 2025; CERT Polska disclosure 8 Aug 2026; press analysis 11 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] Clop’s PLM extortion campaign names Shell, GE and Philips — and the stolen material is plant drawings and blueprints
item.description: Clop has listed more than 50 organisations tied to its exploitation of internet-exposed PTC Windchill and FlexPLM, the product lifecycle management platforms used across aerospace, defence, automotive, heavy machinery, medtech and process industry. Shell confirmed on 14 August that it is investigating a potential incident after the gang claimed 89 GB; GE said it is assessing a claim of 391 GB; Philips confirmed a contained compromise with no impact on customer environments against a claim of 13.5 GB. The advertised inventory is backups, project plans, facility photographs, drawings, diagrams and blueprints. The entry point is CVE-2026-12569, an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw in Windchill and FlexPLM rated CVSS 9.8 and reached through deserialisation of untrusted data. No OT or control-system impact has been reported at any victim — this is confidentiality loss, not disruption. The OT relevance is what was taken: PLM holds the as-designed record of your plants, machines and safety systems, and in most organisations it is neither inventoried as an OT-adjacent asset nor covered by an OT threat model. An adversary who has your drawings does not need your network to plan against you. - Company statements from Shell, GE and Philips; PTC advisory — via BleepingComputer, IndustryWeek, Smart Industry, eSecurity Planet - Shell confirmation 14 Aug 2026; GE and Philips responses 17–18 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Ransomware at Winnipeg’s Health Sciences Centre took down door access, lifts and central HVAC monitoring
item.description: Manitoba’s largest hospital discovered a ransomware attack on 10 August that landed on its facility management systems rather than its clinical estate. Central monitoring of heating, ventilation and cooling was lost, door access and ID card operations were disrupted, and lifts were affected, forcing local monitoring and manual workarounds while teams restored services. Shared Health said in a 17 August update that patient care was not affected. The mechanical plant kept running — what failed was the supervisory layer that watches it and the access control that governs who can reach it. For anyone who has argued that building automation sits outside the OT programme, this is the counter-example to hand to a sceptical executive: a compromise that never touched a clinical system still degraded the physical operation of a Level I facility for days, and the recovery ran on people walking round with keys. - Shared Health Manitoba statements and CBC News reporting — via BankInfoSecurity, DataBreaches.net, Packetlabs - Discovered 10 Aug 2026; health authority update 17 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] A cyberattack stopped goods leaving eight Ceva warehouses — and the outage ran for weeks
item.description: Ceva Logistics, the contract-logistics arm of CMA CGM, had its European operations disrupted on 29 July and was still restoring services nearly two weeks later. Eight warehouses were affected; on 1 August the company told customers that goods held at those sites were not shipping. The downstream list is the interesting part — Dutch retailer Bol, department store De Bijenkorf, eyewear firm Ace & Tate, ING, football club Ajax and Valve’s European hardware business all confirmed impact, several of them also reporting that order and delivery data may have been copied. Ceva says its air, ocean, ground and rail transport management ran normally throughout, so this was contained to contract logistics. Nothing points at warehouse control systems: the conveyors and sorters were not the target. Order processing was, and without it a fulfilment centre is a building full of stock nobody can release. - Ceva customer notifications and statements from Bol, De Bijenkorf and Valve — reported by SecurityWeek, The Record, The Register and Security Affairs - Disruption began 29 Jul 2026; customers notified 1 Aug 2026; still restoring as of reporting 11–12 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Forescout counted 4,407 internet-facing Rockwell controllers — and found 22 of them in the cities that were attacked
item.description: Vedere Labs ran an internet-wide scan on 3 August and published on 5–6 August: 4,407 Rockwell Automation and Allen-Bradley PLCs answering on EtherNet/IP port 44818 worldwide, 2,844 of them in the United States. Twenty-two sat in cities hit by the water-utility attacks. Nineteen of those 22 appear to run firmware susceptible to CVE-2017-16740, a stack-based buffer overflow in MicroLogix 1400 Series B and C on revision 21.002 and earlier, fixed nine years ago in 21.003. The finding that should change how you hunt is the network path: nineteen of the 22 sat on the same mobile carrier network. This exposure is cellular, not corporate. These are field-deployed controllers at pump stations, lift stations and water towers, backhauled to SCADA over cellular modems that hand them public IP addresses — which means they never appear in a corporate firewall rule review, and your network team may have no record they exist. Forescout also found the usual companions around the same utilities: expired TLS certificates, abandoned remote-access hostnames and forgotten servers. - Forescout Vedere Labs research — via The Hacker News, CyberScoop, Cloud Security Alliance research note - Scan conducted 3 Aug 2026; findings published 5–6 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Head Mare broke a videoconferencing server and shipped backdoored client installers to industrial firms
item.description: Kaspersky detected activity in July 2026 in which the Head Mare group chained vulnerabilities in unpatched TrueConf videoconferencing servers — tracked as KLCERT-26-057 and KLCERT-26-058, both giving arbitrary code execution with elevated privileges — to replace the legitimate client installers the server distributes with trojanised builds. Users installing what their own corporate server offered them received the PhantomCore backdoor, which handles reconnaissance, credential theft and command and control, and in some cases PhantomGraph, which routes its command traffic through Microsoft OneDrive to blend with normal cloud usage. Targeting spanned instrumentation, electronics, transport, energy, IT and software development companies. Affected versions run to 5.3.9, 5.4.9 and 5.5.5, which the vendor patched on 18 June. The lesson generalises well beyond one product: any internally hosted platform that distributes signed client software — conferencing, remote support, engineering toolchains, HMI runtime deployment — is a trusted distribution point, and compromising it converts your own patch process into the delivery mechanism. - Kaspersky Securelist research — via The Hacker News, BleepingComputer, SC Media - Activity detected July 2026; vendor patches 18 Jun 2026; research published 20 Aug 2026; CISA KEV addition 20 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Team82 chained 23 flaws in Copeland refrigeration controllers to root, then warmed a fridge while the display kept reading normal
item.description: Claroty’s Team82 disclosed 23 vulnerabilities in the Copeland XWEB Pro supervisory controller family — XWEB300D PRO and XWEB500D PRO — 21 of them rated high severity. The chain starts with a logic flaw in the device’s Lua-based authentication middleware: because any Lua table, including an empty one, evaluates as true, supplying an unrecognised auth_mode returns an empty-but-truthy object and the router waves the request through to the administrative API. A separate predictable password-generation routine yields a deterministic daily administrator credential, giving a second way in. From there Team82 found 19 OS command-injection issues across API and CGI endpoints, all running with elevated privileges, for root-level remote code execution. The part that should interest engineers is the physical demonstration: from a compromised XWEB the researchers drove a serially connected XR60CX field controller over Modbus, disabled the compressor and cooling fans, and simultaneously fed the display the probe’s legitimate reading — so the load spoiled while the temperature record, the same record kept for regulatory compliance, looked clean. Copeland worked with the researchers and shipped firmware 1.13. - Industrial Cyber report on Claroty Team82 research (Amir Zaltzman, Team82 Research blog) - Team82 research published 9 Aug 2026; press coverage 12 Aug 2026; fixed in firmware 1.13

item.title: [Critical] Siemens ships ten advisories, including a maximum-severity missing-authentication flaw in SIMATIC IoT2050
item.description: The August ICS Patch Tuesday round from Siemens, Schneider Electric and Phoenix Contact is led by a maximum-severity missing-authentication vulnerability in Siemens SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced devices, allowing a remote unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on the underlying server with elevated privileges. A critical code-execution flaw in Siveillance Video Management Servers follows — a physical security platform that in many plants sits on the same network as the process. Siemens published ten advisories in total, with high-severity issues in Solid Edge, Simcenter Nastran, Siemens License Server, Simcenter Femap, Parasolid and LOGO! Soft Comfort permitting application crashes, arbitrary code execution, privilege escalation, arbitrary file reads or information disclosure. Most of that second tier is engineering-tier software rather than controller firmware, which changes the exposure but not the consequence: an engineering workstation is the shortest path to controller logic in any plant, and the S7 advisory published eight days later is a reminder that controller logic is what the current campaign is after. - Siemens ProductCERT, Schneider Electric CPCERT and Phoenix Contact advisories — via SecurityWeek - Published 11 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] A CVSS 10.0 unauthenticated code-execution flaw in Entra ID was exploited before disclosure — and there is nothing for you to patch
item.description: CVE-2026-69836 is an unsafe-deserialisation flaw in Microsoft Entra ID that allowed an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute code against the service, scored CVSS 3.1 10.0 with no privileges and no user interaction required. Microsoft disclosed it on 20 August and has said it was exploited in the wild before the fix. Because Entra ID is a Microsoft-operated cloud service, the remediation was applied on Microsoft’s own infrastructure — there is no KB, no package and no configuration change for customers, and the advisory was published for transparency rather than action. That is precisely why it belongs on an OT board. Entra ID is the identity plane behind the VPN concentrators, remote-access portals, jump hosts and vendor accounts that reach most plant networks, so a service-side compromise window is a window against every downstream authentication decision made during it — and unlike an appliance CVE, you cannot close it, verify it or schedule it. The only thing available to you is evidence. - Microsoft Security Response Center advisory — via Help Net Security, The Hacker News, SecurityWeek - Disclosed 20 Aug 2026; exploitation reported 21 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] Citrix patches a CVSS 9.3 authentication bypass in NetScaler Gateway — the box that fronts most third-party OT access
item.description: CVE-2026-19490, disclosed on 19 August, lets an unauthenticated remote attacker bypass authentication through an alternate path on NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway appliances, with no user interaction and no privileges required. Exposure depends on configuration: the appliance must be running as a Gateway — covering SSL VPN, ICA Proxy, CVPN or RDP Proxy — or as an AAA virtual server, and on newer firmware a SAML action must also be configured, while on older firmware the Gateway or AAA role alone is sufficient. Fixed builds are 14.1-73.32 and 13.1-63.21. No in-the-wild exploitation had been observed at disclosure, but researchers are explicit that Citrix appliances historically move from advisory to mass exploitation quickly, and the reason this belongs on an OT board rather than an IT one is positional: NetScaler Gateway is very often the front door through which integrators, OEMs and maintenance contractors reach the plant. An authentication bypass there is an authentication bypass into your remote-access path. - Citrix security bulletin and Rapid7 analysis — via Help Net Security, SecurityWeek, The Hacker News - Advisory published 19 Aug 2026; vendor guidance reiterated 21 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] FUXA, the free web SCADA/HMI that turns up in small plants everywhere, has an unauthenticated RCE chain under active exploitation
item.description: Frangoteam’s FUXA is open-source, browser-based SCADA/HMI software, and its low cost has put it into a great many small utilities, pilot plants, OEM skids and integrator demos that never appear on a corporate asset register. A cluster of vulnerabilities gives unauthenticated remote attackers code execution by more than one route: CVE-2026-25938 bypasses authentication so requests reach the underlying Node-RED execution engine when that plugin is active; CVE-2026-25895 combines missing authentication on a critical function with path traversal in the upload API to write arbitrary files and achieve RCE; CVE-2026-25939 allows unauthenticated creation, modification and deletion of scheduler entries, which is control-system manipulation in its own right before it is ever escalated to code execution. Exploitation attempts against FUXA have been observed, and CISA added a related FUXA flaw to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 19 August with a federal remediation deadline of 2 September. Fixes are in version 1.2.11. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-181-02 and KEV catalogue, GitHub Advisory Database, Frangoteam release notes - KEV addition 19 Aug 2026, federal remediation deadline 2 Sep 2026; fixes in 1.2.11

item.title: [High] Four fresh KEV entries land on infrastructure that sits directly beneath OT: IKE VPN, SharePoint, vCenter and macOS screen sharing
item.description: CISA added four vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 18 August after confirming active attacks, with a federal remediation deadline of 21 August. The set is a wormable double-free in the Microsoft Internet Key Exchange service extensions — the component behind IPsec VPN termination — alongside a SharePoint authentication bypass, a VMware vCenter path traversal and a macOS Screen Sharing authentication bypass. This followed three additions on 11 August, which included Cisco Secure Firewall ASA and FTD issues, and was followed on 20 August by two TrueConf Server entries — CVE-2026-72529 and CVE-2026-72530 — tied to the trojanised-installer campaign against industrial firms covered below. The run of confirmed exploitation stays concentrated on edge, VPN, virtualisation and internally hosted collaboration infrastructure. None of these are ICS products. All four sit under industrial environments in the layer that Dragos’ Q2 data identifies as the actual disruption path: vCenter runs your virtualised HMIs and historians, IKE terminates the tunnels your remote sites and vendors arrive through, and SharePoint holds the procedures and drawings you would need during a recovery. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue additions - Added 18 Aug 2026; federal remediation deadline 21 Aug 2026; prior batch 11 Aug 2026; two further additions 20 Aug 2026

item.title: [Medium] CISA’s one new ICS advisory this week is a fire-alarm management console that holds credentials in cleartext memory
item.description: ICSA-26-232-01, published 20 August, covers Johnson Controls Simplex Incident Manager at version 2.01 and earlier. Tracked as CVE-2026-27875, the flaw is cleartext storage of sensitive information in memory: while the application runs, user passwords and authentication tokens sit unencrypted in process memory, so a local attacker with low privileges who can dump that memory recovers working credentials for the application and for the systems connected to it. Johnson Controls has issued a fixed release — confirm the exact target version against the vendor bulletin before scheduling the change. CISA lists the product as deployed worldwide across critical manufacturing, commercial facilities, government facilities, transportation systems and energy. The reason to care is where this console sits. Incident Manager federates fire panels across a whole estate, so credentials taken from it are credentials to the life-safety network — the OT nobody puts on the OT asset register, usually managed by facilities rather than by the plant, and frequently running on a shared workstation that several people and a remote support contract can reach. That shared workstation is exactly the local access the vulnerability needs. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-232-01 and Johnson Controls product bulletin - Published 20 Aug 2026

item.title: [Info] DESNZ briefs energy chief executives and says sector cyber regulations are being updated
item.description: The most consequential part of the UK generator story for anyone who operates energy assets is not the incident, it is the regulatory response. DESNZ has briefed energy-sector chief executives, issued written guidance on strengthening defences, and officials have indicated that cybersecurity regulations for the sector are being updated. The trigger is instructive: the affected site fell well below the legal threshold at which significant generators must report cyber incidents, and the government source’s own framing was that its capacity was a rounding error against the grid. In other words, the asset that produced a national-level policy response was one the regime had deliberately excluded. Any operator running distributed or small-scale generation should read this as advance notice that the reporting threshold, and likely the associated control expectations, are about to move downward. No draft text or timetable has been published. - UK Department for Energy Security and Net Zero statements — via Irish Times, IBTimes UK - Reported 23 Aug 2026

item.title: [Info] The legal cover for threat-intelligence sharing expires on 30 September, five weeks out
item.description: The Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 provides the statutory framework, liability protections and legal safeguards under which private organisations share cyber threat indicators and defensive measures with federal agencies and one another. Congress extended it through 30 September 2026 in the appropriations act enacted in February, following a lapse and a run of short-term renewals. That date is now five weeks away, and while there is congressional interest in a longer reauthorisation, nothing has passed. For critical-infrastructure operators the practical exposure sits in the ISAC relationship: the E-ISAC, WaterISAC and Food and Ag-ISAC channels that carry sector-specific OT threat information depend on participants being comfortable that sharing carries protection. The uncertainty is itself the operational problem — counsel who cannot rely on the framework tend to advise sharing less, and the effect shows up before the deadline rather than after it. - Congressional Research Service and legal analyses of the February 2026 extension - Forward-looking — statutory sunset 30 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] The Cyber Resilience Act’s vulnerability-management standards are due for adoption on 30 August — and IEC 62443 is the reference
item.description: The standardisation programme underpinning the EU Cyber Resilience Act sets 30 August 2026 as the latest date for adoption of the horizontal Type A standard and the Type B standards covering vulnerability management. For industrial equipment this is the point at which the CRA stops being an abstraction: IEC 62443 is emerging as the key technical reference for CRA compliance in industrial settings, which means the standard many operators have used as a voluntary maturity model becomes the yardstick their suppliers are measured against in a regulated conformity process. The direction of travel is that manufacturers carry more responsibility for what happens to a product after it ships — coordinated disclosure, security updates through a defined support period, and an SBOM. Asset owners are not the regulated party here, but they are the beneficiary, and the leverage arrives at procurement rather than in the plant. - EU Cyber Resilience Act standardisation request status reporting and industrial compliance analyses - Forward-looking — standards adoption deadline 30 Aug 2026

item.title: [Info] A Senate bill would give the EPA explicit authority to inspect water-utility cybersecurity and compel fixes
item.description: The legislative answer to the water campaign now has text. Senators Adam Schiff and Amy Klobuchar introduced the Water Cyber Shield Act on 10 August, and its contents matter to any US drinking-water or wastewater operator regardless of how the bill fares. It would let the EPA carry out cybersecurity assessments and require corrective action where it finds significant weaknesses; direct the EPA, working with CISA and NIST, to set tiered cybersecurity standards scaled to utility size; fold cyber risk formally into the risk-and-resilience assessments large systems already file; extend federal incident-reporting duties to state and municipally owned systems currently exempt; add $300 million a year to the State Revolving Funds earmarked for cyber work; and shield submitted security detail from public-records disclosure. The gap it targets is a real one: the EPA is the sector risk-management agency for water but has never had clear authority to mandate cyber controls, which is why an earlier attempt at binding guidance was withdrawn after legal challenge. Nothing is in force. A bill at introduction is not a requirement, and no committee action has been scheduled. - Water Cyber Shield Act bill text and summary — US Senate sponsor release - Introduced 10 Aug 2026
